translations.text: [?] ...doubted the gifts in this wide world. There she readily found protection from the glorious Prince when she had the greatest need: the grace of the highest Judge, so that he, the Ruler of creation, kept her safe against the greatest terror.
The Father in the heavens, glorious in spirit, granted her this favour because she always had firm faith in the Almighty.
I have heard that Holofernes then eagerly sent out invitations to wine and prepared a feast in splendour, with every kind of wonder.
The lord of men commanded all his most senior thegns to come to it. They did so in great haste: the shield-warriors came travelling to the mighty prince, the leader of the people.
That was on the fourth day after Judith, wise in thought, the woman of elfin beauty, had first come to him.
Then they went to sit at the feast, proud men to the wine-drinking, all his companions in woe, bold warriors in mail-coats.

There deep bowls were carried again and again along the benches, and cups and pitchers too, full, to those sitting in the hall. They took the drink, doomed men, brave shield-warriors, though the powerful one did not expect it, the fearsome lord of nobles.

Then Holofernes, gold-friend of men, grew merry with the pouring of wine. He laughed and shouted, roared and made a din, so that the children of men could hear from far away how the stern-minded one stormed and yelled, arrogant and flushed with mead. Again and again he urged those sitting on the benches to enjoy themselves well.

So all day long the wicked one, the stout-hearted giver of treasure, drenched his retainers with wine, until they lay in a stupor. He made his whole troop of veterans so drunk that they lay as if struck down by death, drained of every good.
So the lord of men ordered the hall-sitters to be served until dark night drew near to the children of men.
Then, filled with malice, he ordered the blessed maiden to be fetched quickly to his bed, laden with bracelets, adorned with rings.
The attendants acted quickly, as their lord, the chief of the mail-coated warriors, had commanded them. They went noisily to the guest-hall, where they found Judith, wise of spirit,
and then the shield-warriors promptly began to lead the radiant maiden to the high tent, where the mighty one always rested at night inside: Holofernes, hateful to the Saviour.
A beautiful, all-golden fly-net was hung there around the commander's bed, so that the wicked one, the lord of warriors, could look through it
at every one of the sons of men who came in there, while no one of humankind could look at him, unless the proud one ordered one of his men bold in hostility to come nearer to him for counsel.
Then they quickly brought the wise woman to the bed. Then the stout-hearted men went to tell their lord that the holy woman had been brought into his pavilion.
Then the famous one, the lord of cities, became glad in mind. He intended to defile the radiant woman with filth and with sin.
But the Judge of glory, the Guardian of majesty, would not allow it. Instead he kept him from that deed: the Lord, ruler of hosts.
Then the devilish one, lustful and wicked, went with a troop of men to seek his bed, where he was to lose his glory swiftly, within a single night.
Then he had met an unpleasant end on earth, such as he had worked for before, the harsh-minded prince of men, while he lived in this world under the roof of the clouds.
Then the mighty one fell down in the middle of his bed, so drunk with wine that he had no sense left in his mind.
The warriors went out of the chamber in great haste, men sated with wine, who had led the oath-breaker, the hateful tyrant, to bed for the last time.
Then the Saviour's handmaid, full of glory, was keenly intent on how she could most easily take the terrible one's life before the foul, sinful man woke up.

Then the curly-haired maiden of the Creator took a sharp sword, hardened in the storms of battle, and drew it from the sheath with her right hand. Then she began to call by name on the Guardian of heaven, the Saviour of all the world's inhabitants, and spoke these words:
"God of creation and Spirit of comfort, Son of the Almighty, I want to pray to you for your mercy on me in my need, Glory of the Trinity.
My heart is now fiercely inflamed and my mind is sad, sorely troubled with sorrows.
Grant me, Lord of heaven, victory and true faith, so that with this sword I may cut down this giver of murder. Grant me my salvation, stern-minded Prince of men.
I have never had greater need of your mercy. Avenge now, mighty Lord, glorious-minded giver of glory, what so angers my mind and burns hot in my breast."
Then the highest Judge at once filled her with courage, as he does for every one of those dwelling here who seeks him for help with wisdom and with right faith.
Then her mind grew easy, and the holy woman's hope was renewed. Then she seized the heathen man firmly by his hair,
pulled him shamefully towards her with her hands, and skilfully laid the wicked one out, the hateful man, so that she could most easily control the wretch.
Then the curly-haired woman struck the hostile enemy, the hate-minded one, with the gleaming sword, so that she cut halfway through his neck, and he lay unconscious, drunk and wounded.
He was not yet dead, not entirely lifeless. Then the courageous woman struck the heathen hound hard a second time, so that his head rolled forward onto the floor.

The foul body lay behind, lifeless; the spirit went elsewhere, under the deep headland, and there it was cast down, fettered in torment forever after, wound about with serpents, bound in punishments, cruelly imprisoned in the burning of hell after his departure.

He need not hope at all, wrapped in darkness, that he may get out of that hall of serpents. Instead he shall stay there for ever and ever, without end, from then on, in that dark home, without the joys of hope.
Judith had then won surpassing glory in battle, as God granted her, the Lord of heaven, who gave her victory.
Then the wise maiden quickly put the warrior's head, all bloody, into the bag in which her attendant, the pale-cheeked woman, had carried the food for both of them,
excellent in her ways, had brought it there; and she then gave it, gory as it was, into the hand of her thoughtful servant to carry home — Judith gave it to her handmaid.

Then the two women, bold in courage, went straight on from there, until they came, elated in spirit, the triumphant maidens, out from the army, so that they could clearly see the walls of the beautiful city shining, Bethulia.
Then, adorned with rings, they hurried on along the footpath until, glad at heart, they had reached the rampart gate.
The warriors sat; the men kept watch and guard in the fortress, as Judith had earlier commanded the sad-hearted people when she set out on her journey, the shrewd-minded maiden, the courageous lady.

Then the beloved one had come back to her people, and at once the wise-minded woman ordered one of the men of the spacious city to come out to meet her, and they quickly let them in through the gate of the wall,
and spoke these words to the victorious people: "I can tell you something to be thankful for: you need not mourn in your hearts any longer.

The Creator, the glory of kings, is gracious to you. It has been made known far and wide throughout the world that splendid glorious success is coming to you, and glory is granted to you for the injuries you have long suffered."
Then the people living in the city were glad, once they heard how the holy one spoke over the high wall. The army rejoiced.

The people hurried toward the fortress gate, men and women together, in crowds and masses, in throngs and troops. They pressed forward and ran by the thousands to meet the Lord's maiden, old and young.
The heart of every man in that mead-city was gladdened when they saw that Judith had come back to her homeland, and they quickly and humbly let her in.
then the wise one, adorned with gold, ordered her attentive handmaid to unwrap the warrior's head and show it, bloody, as a sign to the townspeople of how she had fared in battle.
Then the noble one spoke to all the people: "Here, victorious heroes, leaders of the people, you can see clearly and gaze on the head of the most hateful heathen warrior,

of the lifeless Holofernes, who of all men did us the most murders, grievous sorrows, and wished to increase that still more; but God did not grant him longer life, that he might afflict us with harms;
I deprived him of life through God's help. Now I wish to ask every man of these townspeople, you shield-warriors, that you at once hasten to battle.

As soon as the God of creation, the gracious King, sends the bright light from the east, bear forth your linden shields, boards before your breasts, and mail coats, bright helmets, into the throng of the ravagers; cut down the leaders with shining swords, the doomed chieftains.
Your enemies are condemned to death, and you shall have glory, honour in the fight, as the mighty Lord has shown you through my hand."
Then a troop of the brave was quickly made ready, of the bold for battle.
The nobly brave men and retainers marched out, bore victory banners, went forth straight to battle, heroes under helmets, from the holy city at the very break of dawn.
Shields resounded, clashed loudly. At that the lean wolf in the forest rejoiced, and the dark raven, the slaughter-greedy bird.
Both knew that the men of the nation meant to provide them a feast on the doomed; and behind them flew the eagle, eager for food, dewy-feathered; the dark-coated, horn-beaked one sang a battle song.
The warriors marched, men to battle, covered by shields, by curved linden boards — those who a while before had endured the taunts of foreigners, the scorn of heathens.
This was harshly paid back to all of them, the Assyrians, in the play of ash-spears, after the Hebrews had marched under their battle-banners to the army camps.
Then they boldly let fly showers of arrows, battle-adders, from horn bows, firm hard shafts; the fierce warriors roared loudly and sent spears into the throng of the hardy foe.
The heroes, the dwellers in the land, were angry at the hateful race; they marched stern-minded, stout-hearted, and roughly roused their ancient enemies, drowsy with mead;

With their hands the warriors drew brightly adorned swords from their sheaths, swords with proven edges. Grimly they struck the Assyrian warriors, who had hostile intentions. They spared none of that army, neither lowly nor powerful, none of the living men they could overcome.
So the young retainers pursued the foreigners all through that morning, until those who were hostile, the army's chief guards, realized that the Hebrew men were showing them fierce sword-strokes.

They went to report this in words to the most senior chief officers. They roused the standard-bearing warriors and fearfully announced the sudden news to them: to the mead-weary men, a morning terror, a dreadful play of swords.
Then at once, I have heard, the warriors doomed to die shook off sleep, and with weary hearts they crowded in throngs toward the pavilion of the evil one, Holofernes.
They meant to announce the battle to their lord immediately, before the terror, the might of the Hebrews, came down upon him.
They all supposed that the lord of warriors and the radiant maiden were together in the beautiful tent: Judith the noble and the lustful one, terrible and fierce.
Yet there was none of the nobles who dared to wake the warrior or find out how things had gone between the banner-warrior and the holy maiden, the Lord's woman.
The force drew near, the people of the Hebrews; they fought fiercely with hard battle-weapons, and with sword-hilts, with shining swords, paid back their ancient quarrels, their old grudges;
Through that day's work the glory of the Assyrians was diminished and their pride brought low. The warriors stood around their lord's tent, greatly agitated and dark in spirit.
Then all of them together began to cough, to cry out loudly and to gnash their teeth. Stripped of all good, they suffered their grief by grinding their teeth.
Then their glory, their prosperity and their brave deeds were at an end. The men thought to wake their lord and friend, but it did them no good at all.
Then at last, slowly and late, one of the warriors grew bold enough, hardened in battle, to venture into the pavilion, as necessity drove him.
There on the bed he found his gold-giver lying pale, empty of spirit, deprived of life.
At once he fell, chilled, to the ground. Fierce in mind, he began to tear his hair and his clothes as well, and he spoke these words to the warriors who were outside there, downcast:
"Here our own destruction is made plain. It is shown that the time is coming, now pressed close upon us with troubles, when we must of necessity perish and be destroyed together in battle.
Here our lord lies cut down by the sword, beheaded." Then, sorrowful in mind, they threw down their weapons and, weary in spirit, hurried away in flight.

A mighty people fought them from behind, until the greatest part of the army lay felled in battle on the field of victory, hewn down by swords, a pleasure to the wolves and also a comfort to the slaughter-greedy birds.

Those who were still alive fled, the shield-bearing troop of the hated enemy. Behind them came the Hebrew army, honoured with victory and exalted in glory. The Lord God, the almighty Lord, came graciously to their help.
Then boldly, with gleaming swords, the brave-hearted warriors cut a path for the army through the throng of their enemies. They hewed the linden-wood shields and cut through the shield-wall.

The fighters, the Hebrew men, were roused to battle. At that time the warriors were fiercely eager for the clash of spears. There the greatest part of the whole count of the Assyrian nobility, that hated race, fell onto the dust.
Few of the living came back to their homeland. The warriors, bold as kings, turned back on the return path, through the carnage and the reeking corpses.

The people of the land had ample opportunity to take from the most hated foe, their old enemies now lifeless: the bloody war-gear, beautiful ornaments, shields and broadswords, gleaming helmets, precious treasures.

The defenders of the homeland had gloriously overcome their enemies on that battlefield and put their old foes to sleep with swords. Those who, of all living peoples, had been most hateful to them in life lay at rest along their track.
Then for the space of one month the whole nation, the most glorious of tribes, proud and curly-haired, carried and led to the bright city of Bethulia
helmets and hip-swords, grey mail-coats, men's war-gear adorned with gold, more splendid treasures than any man of shrewd mind could tell;
…everything that the men of the nation, bold under their banners, had won gloriously in battle through the wise counsel of Judith, the courageous maiden.
As a reward, the spear-brave warriors brought back to her from that expedition Holofernes's sword and bloody helmet, and also his broad coat of mail adorned with red gold,
and all that the strong-minded prince of warriors had owned of riches or private wealth, of rings and bright treasures, they gave it to that bright lady, ready of mind.
For all of this Judith gave glory to the Lord of hosts, who had given her honour and fame in the kingdom of the earth, and also reward in heaven,
the prize of victory in the glory of the sky, because she had true faith in the Almighty. Indeed, at the end she did not doubt the reward she had long desired.
For this be glory for ever and ever to the beloved Lord, who created wind and air, the heavens and the wide earth, and also the raging seas and the joys of heaven, through his own mercy.
